deletion_policy.description:
Whether Terraform will be prevented from destroying the instance. Defaults to "DELETE".
When a 'terraform destroy' or 'terraform apply' would delete the instance,
the command will fail if this field is set to "PREVENT" in Terraform state.
When set to "ABANDON", the command will remove the resource from Terraform
management without updating or deleting the resource in the API.
When set to "DELETE", deleting the resource is allowed.
deletion_policy.rationale: A policy should be set for this to either be PREVENT or ABANDON as this will prevent a user from accidentally deleting and any firewall policy that may be protecting the network.

description.description: An optional description of this resource.
description.rationale: No security impact as its purley for the developers to note anything down.

name.description:
User-provided name of the Network firewall policy.
The name should be unique in the project in which the firewall policy is created.
The name must be 1-63 characters long, and comply with RFC1035. Specifically,
the name must be 1-63 characters long and match the regular expression [a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?
which means the first character must be a lowercase letter, and all following characters must be a dash,
lowercase letter, or digit, except the last character, which cannot be a dash.
name.rationale: This is a user provided name for the firewall policy, we dont constrain names with their resources (too overreaching)

policy_type.description:
Policy type is used to determine which resources (networks) the policy can be associated with.
A policy can be associated with a network only if the network has the matching policyType in its network profile.
Different policy types may support some of the Firewall Rules features. Possible values: ["VPC_POLICY", "RDMA_ROCE_POLICY", "RDMA_FALCON_POLICY", "ULL_POLICY"]
policy_type.rationale: There are four possible policy type values: 'VPC_POLICY' 'RDMA_ROCE_POLICY' 'RDMA_FALCON_POLICY' 'ULL_POLICY', These are design considerations and not security related, if we restrict these we are restricting the developers ability to design their firewall policies.

project.description: The ID of the project in which the resource belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
project.rationale: This specifies the Google Cloud project which contains this resource. A platform policy should not restrict such project identiifiers.

region.rationale: Determines the region/zone where the resource is created. Policy should restrict it to an approved-region whitelist for data residency; the allowed set is parameterised (a hardcoded example whitelist is acceptable).

rule.description: A list of firewall policy rules.

rule.action.description:
The Action to perform when the client connection triggers the rule. Can currently be either
"allow", "deny", "apply_security_profile_group" or "goto_next".
rule.action.rationale: This action determines if matched traffic is permitted, blocked, inspected or passed on. This shoulden't be restricted as it hinders how a team can build their firewall. A policy that requires a particular action will be dictating how access works and therefore this is out of the scope of security.

rule.description.rationale: Descriptive only and has no impact on security.

rule.direction.description: The direction in which this rule applies. If unspecified an INGRESS rule is created. Possible values: ["INGRESS", "EGRESS"]
rule.direction.rationale: This sets the direction of the rule (inbound/outbound) traffic, we cant restrict this using a policy as there is no security impact at all. Developers should have the ability to write firewall rules freely (too overreaching).

rule.disabled.description:
Denotes whether the firewall policy rule is disabled. When set to true,
the firewall policy rule is not enforced and traffic behaves as if it did
not exist. If this is unspecified, the firewall policy rule will be
enabled.
rule.disabled.rationale: When this is set to true, the rule can still exist in the configuration but is not inforced. Policy should require rules to be enabled.

rule.enable_logging.description:
Denotes whether to enable logging for a particular rule.
If logging is enabled, logs will be exported to the
configured export destination in Stackdriver.
rule.enable_logging.rationale: This ensures that any permitted/blocked traffic that triggers the rule is logged allowing us to have an audit trail for detection, forensics and incident response. A policy should be written to ensure that it is enabled for logging and auditing.

rule.priority.description:
An integer indicating the priority of a rule in the list. The priority must be a value
between 0 and 2147483647. Rules are evaluated from highest to lowest priority where 0 is the
highest priority and 2147483647 is the lowest priority.
rule.priority.rationale: Ordering the value of the rule does not impact security and this should be a design choice by the developer. We have no effective way of telling if a rule is of a higher priority than another which therefore this has no security impact.

rule.rule_name.description:
An optional name for the rule. This field is not a unique identifier
and can be updated.
rule.rule_name.rationale: No security impact as this is purley descriptive.

rule.security_profile_group.description:
A fully-qualified URL of a SecurityProfile resource instance.
Example:
https://networksecurity.googleapis.com/v1/projects/{project}/locations/{location}/securityProfileGroups/my-security-profile-group
Must be specified if action is 'apply_security_profile_group'.
rule.security_profile_group.rationale: A security profile group attaches advanced traffic inspection (IDS, anti-malware and URL filtering) to the rule, which is a higher-assurance feature tier rather than a plain allow/deny decision. This falls under the whitelist secure tiers/features archetype: where traffic inspection is mandated, policy should require rules to reference a security profile group (and correspondingly use the 'apply_security_profile_group' action). The set of approved profile groups is parameterised rather than hardcoded.

rule.target_service_accounts.description:
A list of service accounts indicating the sets of
instances that are applied with this rule.
rule.target_service_accounts.rationale: This field is an IAM-based scoping reference to existing service accounts that determines which instances the rule applies to. It references existing resources rather than defining or naming new resources, so we do not constrain the service account names or references used here.

rule.tls_inspect.description:
Boolean flag indicating if the traffic should be TLS decrypted.
It can be set only if action = 'apply_security_profile_group' and cannot be set for other actions.
rule.tls_inspect.rationale: TLS Inspection should be used when a security profile group is attached, otherwise the firewall will have no way to enforce any security profiles that may be present. If there isnt a security profile group set, then TLS inspection shouldent be required. The policy should check if there is a security profile group and force this to be turned on.

rule.match.description: A match condition that incoming traffic is evaluated against. If it evaluates to true, the corresponding 'action' is enforced.

rule.match.dest_address_groups.description:
Address groups which should be matched against the traffic destination.
Maximum number of destination address groups is 10.
rule.match.dest_address_groups.rationale: These values are identifiers referencing separate firewall address group resources. We cannot contrain references or identifiers that point to other resources. Therefore no policy is written here.

rule.match.dest_fqdns.description:
Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) which should be matched against
traffic destination. Maximum number of destination fqdn allowed is 100.
rule.match.dest_fqdns.rationale: Destination FQDN point the rule at a specific external domain. Which domain a team decideds to route to or allow/block is an architecture choice, This therefore means no security policy can be written here.

rule.match.dest_ip_ranges.description:
Destination IP address range in CIDR format. Required for
EGRESS rules.
rule.match.dest_ip_ranges.rationale: Destination CIDR blocks are network address ranges, which per the service-wide guidelines are team addressing and architectural choices. Segmentation is delivered by the firewall rules themselves rather than by constraining range size, and flagging broad ranges such as 0.0.0.0/0 would overreach because many egress rules legitimately require broad or internet-bound destinations.

rule.match.dest_region_codes.description:
Region codes whose IP addresses will be used to match for destination
of traffic. Should be specified as 2 letter country code defined as per
ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes. ex."US"
Maximum number of destination region codes allowed is 5000.
rule.match.dest_region_codes.rationale: This matches traffic destinations by ISO 3166 country code, making it a geolocation control. Data residency and geo-restriction are sanctioned policy targets regardless of whether the resource itself stores data, so restricting which countries workloads may send traffic to is in scope. Policy should require destination region codes to fall within an approved country whitelist, with the allowed set parameterised.

rule.match.dest_threat_intelligences.description:
Names of Network Threat Intelligence lists.
The IPs in these lists will be matched against traffic destination.
rule.match.dest_threat_intelligences.rationale: This is very useful as it checks and prevents a connection to a malicious IP address. A security policy should require this to ensure that there are no communications to malicious IPs, this policy would also ensure if an developer makes a critical error by accidentally entering a malicious IP.

rule.match.src_address_groups.description:
Address groups which should be matched against the traffic source.
Maximum number of source address groups is 10.
rule.match.src_address_groups.rationale: This matches the rule to the address group, a policy has no way of determining if an address group has a security implication and therefore enforcement is not possible. Restricting this would hinder developers.

rule.match.src_fqdns.description:
Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) which should be matched against
traffic source. Maximum number of source fqdn allowed is 100.
rule.match.src_fqdns.rationale: Source FQDN point the rule at a specific external domain. Which domain a team decideds to route to or allow/block is an architecture choice, This therefore means no security policy can be written here.

rule.match.src_ip_ranges.description:
Source IP address range in CIDR format. Required for
INGRESS rules.
rule.match.src_ip_ranges.rationale: Source CIDR blocks are network address ranges used for team segmentation and architectural design, which the service-wide guidelines place outside policy scope. Constraining range size here would substitute platform opinion for the team's own addressing and firewall design

rule.match.src_region_codes.description:
Region codes whose IP addresses will be used to match for source
of traffic. Should be specified as 2 letter country code defined as per
ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes. ex."US"
Maximum number of source region codes allowed is 5000.
rule.match.src_region_codes.rationale: This rule matches traffic sources by ISO 3166 Country code, restricting connections that may originate from the region. Policy should be able to require source region codes to be constrained to an approved country rather than accepting traffic from anywhere.

rule.match.src_threat_intelligences.description:
Names of Network Threat Intelligence lists.
The IPs in these lists will be matched against traffic source.
rule.match.src_threat_intelligences.rationale: This is very useful as it checks and prevents a connection to a malicious IP address. A security policy should require this to ensure that there are no communications to malicious IPs, this policy would also ensure if an developer makes a critical error by accidentally entering a malicious IP.

rule.match.layer4_config.description: Pairs of IP protocols and ports that the rule should match.

rule.match.layer4_config.ip_protocol.description:
The IP protocol to which this rule applies. The protocol
type is required when creating a firewall rule.
This value can either be one of the following well
known protocol strings (tcp, udp, icmp, esp, ah, ipip, sctp),
or the IP protocol number.
rule.match.layer4_config.ip_protocol.rationale: This names the protocol that hte rule matches, this is up to the developer to configure and no security policy is going to be able to tell which known protocol strings a rule will use. This therefore has no security impact.

rule.match.layer4_config.ports.description:
An optional list of ports to which this rule applies. This field
is only applicable for UDP or TCP protocol. Each entry must be
either an integer or a range. If not specified, this rule
applies to connections through any port.
Example inputs include: ["22"], ["80","443"], and
["12345-12349"].
rule.match.layer4_config.ports.rationale: If no port list is supplied the rule applies to connections through every port, which significantly increases the attack surface. Policy should enforce structural limits: require an explicit, non-empty port list on TCP/UDP rules and reject wildcard or excessively broad port ranges. It should not hardcode which specific ports a team may open, as that would constrain their architecture.

rule.match.src_secure_tag.description: List of secure tag values, which should be matched at the source of the traffic. For INGRESS rule, if all the srcSecureTag are INEFFECTIVE, and there is no srcIpRange, this rule will be ignored. Maximum number of source tag values allowed is 256.

rule.match.src_secure_tag.name.description:
Name of the secure tag, created with TagManager's TagValue API.
@pattern tagValues/[0-9]+
rule.match.src_secure_tag.name.rationale: The tag name is created in tag manager used to identify workloads. We have no way of using policy to control what the tag name can be and this therefore is too overreaching and unable to be written as policy.

rule.target_secure_tag.description: A list of secure tags that controls which instances the firewall rule applies to. If targetSecureTag are specified, then the firewall rule applies only to instances in the VPC network that have one of those EFFECTIVE secure tags, if all the target_secure_tag are in INEFFECTIVE state, then this rule will be ignored. targetSecureTag may not be set at the same time as targetServiceAccounts. If neither targetServiceAccounts nor targetSecureTag are specified, the firewall rule applies to all instances on the specified network. Maximum number of target label tags allowed is 256.

rule.target_secure_tag.name.description:
Name of the secure tag, created with TagManager's TagValue API.
@pattern tagValues/[0-9]+
rule.target_secure_tag.name.rationale: The tag name is created in tag manager used to identify workloads. We have no way of using policy to control what the tag name can be and this therefore is too overreaching and unable to be written as policy.
